summary: Satellite networks have topologies in constant motion and links less reliable than terrestrial ones, though some changes can be anticipated from orbits. This informational document proposes a scalable routing architecture for them based on existing routing protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: Satellites keep moving, so the roads between them keep changing. This proposes a way for the network to keep up using tools we already have.

questions: how to route in satellite networks
subtitle: A scalable routing architecture for satellite networks using existing protocols enhanced with orbital link schedules.

tldr.problem: Satellite networks have continuously moving topologies with links far less reliable than terrestrial networks, making conventional routing protocols and scalability approaches inadequate for large constellations.
tldr.mechanism: The architecture proposes using IS-IS with Area Proxy for hierarchical scalability, organizing satellites into stripes (groups of adjacent orbits), using Segment Routing with MPLS for flexible forwarding, and leveraging predictable link connectivity schedules from orbital dynamics.
tldr.outcome: This informational guidance enables deployment of large-scale satellite networks using standards-based routing technology without new protocol changes, though implementation requires validation through simulation and operational deployment.

facts.label: Interior routing protocol
facts.value: IS-IS with Area Proxy and hierarchical L1L2

today: RFC 9717 is an Informational RFC published in January 2025 that presents the author's architectural guidance for satellite routing. It proposes no new protocols or protocol changes; implementation requires validation through simulation and operational deployment with actual satellite operators.

sections.title: The Challenge of Satellite Routing
sections.content:
Satellite networks present unprecedented routing challenges. Unlike terrestrial networks with relatively static topology, satellite networks have topologies in continual motion due to orbital dynamics. Inter-satellite links (ISLs) are less reliable than terrestrial links and can be temporarily unavailable due to range constraints or solar conjunction. Despite this instability, some topological changes are predictable from orbital mechanics and can be scheduled in advance.

Large-scale satellite constellations currently being deployed involve tens of thousands of proposed satellites. Traditional terrestrial routing architectures, designed for static or slowly-changing networks, cannot scale to networks where the entire topology is in constant flux. This RFC proposes a scalable routing architecture based on existing standards-based routing technology (IS-IS and Segment Routing) enhanced with scheduled link connectivity information.
sections.plainLanguage: Satellites zoom around the Earth, so the network links between them are constantly changing. We cannot use the same routing tricks we use for ground networks.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Assumptions
sections.content:
The proposed architecture organizes the satellite constellation with gateways (high-capacity Earth stations that connect to the internet) and user stations (low-capacity endpoints). User stations communicate with satellites, which interconnect via ISLs and forward traffic across the constellation to gateways.

Key assumptions include: the satellite network carries IP traffic through an MPLS-based data plane; satellites actively participate in control and routing protocols; traffic flows primarily from gateways to user stations; and the network is assumed to be connected almost always, even if some links fail. The architecture makes an important observation: unlike terrestrial links, ISL and ground link changes can be anticipated due to orbital dynamics. The network should use a management system to provide scheduled link connectivity information to routing elements.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways are like big hubs on the ground. User stations are small end points. The satellites connect them all, and they know in advance when links will come up or go down because of orbital math.

sections.title: Forwarding Plane and Data Routing
sections.content:
The architecture proposes using MPLS as the fundamental forwarding plane, specifically Segment Routing over MPLS (SR-MPLS). Each satellite is assigned a node Segment Identifier (SID), allowing paths through the network to be expressed as label stacks. This provides flexible and adaptive forwarding critical when topology changes frequently.

User stations on satellites are assigned IP addresses from prefixes managed by their local gateway. Gateways advertise these prefixes globally via BGP so that traffic destined for user stations can reach the appropriate gateway. Forwarding within the satellite network uses SR label stacks rather than IP lookups, allowing the network to recover from unexpected ISL failures by computing new paths to the next waypoint without dropping traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Each satellite gets a label, and packets carry a stack of labels showing the path through satellites. When a link fails, the network finds a new path without losing the packet.

sections.title: Hierarchical Scalability with Stripes and Areas
sections.content:
Achieving scalability in a network with thousands or tens of thousands of satellites requires hierarchical abstraction. The architecture proposes organizing satellites into stripes—groups of a few adjacent orbits that form an IS-IS Level 1 (L1) area. Stripes are connected to other stripes using the same ISL mechanism, forming the Level 2 (L2) topology.

IS-IS with Area Proxy (RFC 9666) enables this hierarchy. Within each stripe, all nodes combine their topological information into a single Link State Protocol Data Unit visible at L2, completely hiding the internal stripe details. This allows the L2 network to scale with the number of stripes, not the number of satellites. For example, a network of 1,000 satellites organized into 1,000 stripes with 1,000 nodes each requires only 1,000 entries in both the L1 and L2 link state databases, a practical scalability level.
sections.plainLanguage: Stripes are clusters of satellites in nearby orbits. They hide their internal roads from other stripes, so the big global network only needs to track roads between stripe clusters, not between individual satellites.

sections.title: Scheduling and Topology Management
sections.content:
The most significant difference between satellite and terrestrial networks is that many topology changes are predictable. A management plane should distribute scheduled link connectivity information to network elements that make routing decisions (L1 nodes for L1 changes, L2 nodes for L2 changes) and to gateways and Path Computation Elements (PCEs).

When a link or satellite is scheduled to join the network, the network should wait for confirmation via normal IS-IS liveness mechanisms before using the new topology. Pre-computation of routes may occur, but new paths should not be installed until the topology is proven operational. When a link or satellite is scheduled to be removed, the network should act proactively before the change: set the link to a high metric to direct traffic around the removal, allowing the network to converge before the actual topology change occurs. This proactive rerouting prevents packet loss during scheduled maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: When we know in advance that a satellite will move out of range or a new link will turn on, we can tell the network ahead of time so it is ready with new roads before the change happens.
